youtube.title: How Much Cash Flow Should a Rental Property Make? ($100 vs $300 vs $500)
youtube.description:
How much monthly cash flow should a rental property actually make?

In this hypothetical EM Property Group breakdown, we compare three rentals producing $100, $300, and $500 per month in cash flow. Then we stress-test each one with the same repair, insurance increase, rent shortfall, and cash-on-cash analysis.

The goal is not to find one magic number. It is to understand how much margin remains when your assumptions are wrong.

If you want simple rental-property analysis without the hype, subscribe to EM Property Group.

Real Estate Investing Made Simple.

#RealEstateInvesting #RentalProperty #CashFlow #RealEstateForBeginners

This is a hypothetical educational example using simplified numbers. Actual returns vary by property, market, financing, taxes, insurance, condition, vacancy, repairs, and other factors. This content is not financial, legal, tax, lending, appraisal, or investment advice.

scenes.title: HOW MUCH CASH FLOW IS ENOUGH?
scenes.narration: Is one hundred dollars a month in rental cash flow enough? What about three hundred? Or five hundred? There is no magic number that works for every investor, but there is a simple way to tell whether your margin is strong enough. In this video, we will compare all three.

scenes.title: WHAT CASH FLOW REALLY MEANS
scenes.narration: First, cash flow is what is left after rent comes in and you subtract the ongoing operating expenses and the mortgage payment. If you collect rent but ignore taxes, insurance, vacancy, maintenance, management, or debt, you are not looking at true cash flow.

scenes.title: THREE HYPOTHETICAL DEALS
scenes.narration: For this hypothetical comparison, imagine three rental properties with similar neighborhoods, condition, and risk. Deal A produces one hundred dollars per month. Deal B produces three hundred. Deal C produces five hundred.

scenes.title: SEE IT ANNUALLY
scenes.narration: On an annual basis, that is twelve hundred dollars for Deal A, thirty-six hundred for Deal B, and six thousand dollars for Deal C. Seeing the annual number makes the difference in margin much easier to understand.

scenes.title: POSITIVE DOESN'T ALWAYS MEAN STRONG
scenes.narration: A beginner may think any positive number is automatically good. But positive cash flow can still be too thin if one repair, one insurance increase, or one rent shortfall wipes out most of the year's profit.
scenes.sub: One repair can erase a thin margin.

scenes.title: $2,400 SURPRISE REPAIR
scenes.narration: So let us stress-test all three deals with the exact same surprise: a twenty-four-hundred-dollar repair.

scenes.title: DEAL A: REPAIR RECOVERY
scenes.narration: At one hundred dollars per month, Deal A needs twenty-four months of projected cash flow to earn back that repair. That is two full years of cash flow.

scenes.title: DEAL B: REPAIR RECOVERY
scenes.narration: At three hundred dollars per month, Deal B needs eight months of projected cash flow to recover the same repair.

scenes.title: DEAL C: REPAIR RECOVERY
scenes.narration: At five hundred dollars per month, Deal C needs just under five months. Same repair. Very different impact.

scenes.title: $50 / MONTH INSURANCE INCREASE
scenes.narration: Now assume insurance increases by fifty dollars per month. Deal A drops from one hundred dollars to only fifty dollars. Half of its projected margin disappears.

scenes.title: DEAL B AFTER INSURANCE SHOCK
scenes.narration: Deal B falls from three hundred to two hundred fifty dollars per month. That hurts, but there is still meaningful breathing room.

scenes.title: DEAL C AFTER INSURANCE SHOCK
scenes.narration: Deal C falls from five hundred to four hundred fifty dollars. The same fifty-dollar increase is much easier for a stronger-margin property to absorb.
scenes.sub: The same shock is easier to absorb.

scenes.title: $50 LOWER RENT
scenes.narration: Now let us say the verified market rent ends up fifty dollars lower than the original projection. Again, every deal loses the same fifty dollars per month, but the weaker deal feels it much more.
scenes.sub: Thin margins feel the same mistake more.

scenes.title: DOUBLE STRESS TEST
scenes.narration: If rent is fifty dollars lower and insurance is fifty dollars higher at the same time, Deal A goes from one hundred dollars to zero. Deal B goes from three hundred to two hundred. Deal C goes from five hundred to four hundred.

scenes.title: THE BETTER QUESTION
scenes.narration: That is the key lesson: the question is not just, is the property cash-flow positive? The better question is, how much room does the property have when your assumptions are wrong?
scenes.sub: Not just: Is cash flow positive?

scenes.title: DON'T IGNORE CASH INVESTED
scenes.narration: The dollar amount is not the only number that matters. You should also compare the cash flow with how much cash you had to invest.

scenes.title: $30,000 CASH INVESTED
scenes.narration: Suppose each deal required thirty thousand dollars of total cash invested. One hundred dollars per month equals twelve hundred per year, or about a four percent annual cash-on-cash return before taxes and other considerations.

scenes.title: $30,000 CASH INVESTED
scenes.narration: Three hundred dollars per month equals thirty-six hundred dollars per year, which is about twelve percent on thirty thousand dollars invested.

scenes.title: $30,000 CASH INVESTED
scenes.narration: Five hundred dollars per month equals six thousand dollars per year, or twenty percent on thirty thousand dollars invested. That looks much stronger, but unusually high returns deserve extra verification because risk or missing expenses may be hiding in the numbers.
scenes.sub: Strong on paper — verify why it's so high.

scenes.title: THERE IS NO UNIVERSAL MINIMUM
scenes.narration: There is no universal minimum cash-flow number. A newer property with low repair risk may justify a different target than an older property with deferred maintenance. A high-cost market may look different from a lower-cost market. Financing and your own reserve position matter too.

scenes.title: EM PROPERTY GROUP FRAMEWORK
scenes.narration: For EM Property Group, I would screen cash flow with five questions: how many dollars remain each month, what is the cash-on-cash return, how much margin survives a stress test, how strong are the reserves, and what property or neighborhood risks are still unknown.

scenes.title: DEAL A SCORE
scenes.narration: Deal A, at one hundred dollars per month, gets a weak score. It is technically positive, but it has very little room for error.

scenes.title: DEAL B SCORE
scenes.narration: Deal B, at three hundred dollars per month, looks workable under these assumptions. It has enough margin to absorb smaller changes without immediately going negative.

scenes.title: DEAL C SCORE
scenes.narration: Deal C, at five hundred dollars per month, looks strongest on cash flow, but we still have to verify why the return is so high and make sure we did not miss expenses, condition problems, or neighborhood risk.

scenes.title: BUILD A SAFETY BUFFER
scenes.narration: Instead of chasing one magic number, set a personal minimum that includes a safety buffer. For example, if your goal is at least two hundred fifty dollars per month after realistic expenses and financing, a deal that only projects two hundred fifty gives you no cushion. You may want the initial projection to be higher.
scenes.sub: If your minimum is $250, don't project exactly $250.

scenes.title: SO… HOW MUCH IS ENOUGH?
scenes.narration: So is one hundred dollars enough? For a deal with normal repair and expense risk, I would consider that a thin margin. Three hundred gives you more breathing room. Five hundred is stronger if the numbers are real. The higher cash flow is not automatically better, but the stronger buffer usually gives you more ways to survive bad assumptions.

scenes.title: 5 TAKEAWAYS
scenes.narration: Five takeaways. One: positive cash flow does not automatically mean a good deal. Two: measure cash flow after realistic expenses and debt. Three: stress-test repairs, rent, and insurance. Four: compare cash flow with cash invested. And five: build a margin above your personal minimum.
items: Compare cash flow to cash invested
